item.title: New Mexico State Police Ends Dangerous Multi-Agency Pursuit with Successful PIT Maneuver
item.description:
Lea County — August 12, 2026 — New Mexico State Police (NMSP) assisted the Lea County Sheriff’s Office in bringing a high-speed pursuit to a safe conclusion after a driver engaged in a series of reckless and dangerous maneuvers that endangered both law enforcement and the public.

The Initial Stop Attempt

The incident began when Lea County Sheriff’s deputies attempted to stop a vehicle for driving recklessly through a school zone and nearly striking another vehicle. When signaled to pull over, the driver immediately fled the scene.

Escalating Danger

What followed was an escalating display of dangerous driving behavior. The fleeing driver traveled at speeds reaching approximately 105 miles per hour and at one point drove westbound in the eastbound lanes of Highway 82, creating an imminent collision hazard for oncoming traffic.

As the pursuit continued onto Highway 457, the driver’s erratic behavior intensified. The driver repeatedly left the roadway, executed multiple U-turns, and came dangerously close to striking oncoming vehicles. During an attempt by officers to deploy stop sticks, the driver allegedly maneuvered the vehicle directly toward a Lea County Sheriff’s deputy before swerving around him at the last moment.

Safe Resolution

An NMSP officer skillfully executed a Precision Intervention Technique (PIT) maneuver, successfully disabling the vehicle and bringing the pursuit to an end. The driver was immediately taken into custody.

Arrest and Charges

The driver, identified as 25-year-old Christina Clayton, was arrested at the scene. Officers observed signs consistent with possible impairment. Clayton has been charged with:

• Speeding

• Reckless Driving

• Aggravated Assault Upon a Peace Officer with a Deadly Weapon

• Two counts of Aggravated Fleeing a Law Enforcement Officer

No Injuries Reported

Despite the dangerous nature of the pursuit and the high speeds involved, no officers or members of the public sustained injuries during the incident.

The New Mexico State Police commended the collaborative efforts of all agencies involved in safely concluding this high-risk situation and protecting the public during a volatile incident.

item.title: Silver Edges Alamogordo in Defensive Battle at Silver City Tournament Friday Evening
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. Alamogordo High School’s boys soccer team suffered a heartbreaking 2-1 defeat to Silver on Saturday in the opening match of the Silver City Round Robin Tournament at Ben Altimirano Soccer Complex.

The match remained scoreless through the first half, with both teams locked in a defensive struggle. The Tigers broke through in the 42nd minute to take a 1-0 lead, but Silver answered back quickly after the intermission, equalizing in the 49th minute on a goal by Kyle Tamayo.

The shift in momentum proved costly for Alamogordo. Silver capitalized on the Tigers’ defensive lapses to score the match-winner and secure the 2-1 victory.

“It’s a tough loss in a tournament setting,” said Tigers head coach following the match. “We had our chances, and we competed hard, but we need to tighten up our defense and convert our opportunities.”

Tamayo’s goal kept the Tigers competitive throughout the second half, but Alamogordo couldn’t find the equalizer despite sustained pressure late in the match.

The loss drops Alamogordo to 0-1 in tournament play. The Tigers will look to bounce back quickly when they face Miyamura later today at 12:30 PM, seeking their first win of the tournament.

The Silver City Round Robin Tournament continues Saturday at Ben Altimirano Soccer Complex reported by Journalist Chris Edwards.

item.title: In Memory of Beth Broughton
item.description:
The spirit of our beloved Connie Beth Broughton returned home to her Heavenly Father on August 1, 2026, at the age of 66. She passed away peacefully at her home in Alamogordo, in the presence of her husband, daughter and son.

Connie was born on April 14, 1960, in Saint George, Utah. She was the sixth and last child of Charles Victor Anderson and Beth (Andrus) Anderson. She is survived by her loving husband of almost 40 years, Collin Broughton, daughter Darla Broughton, son Reece Broughton, brother Dennis (Peggy), brother Craig (Laura), sister Karla Clark (Richard), and brother Brent (Brooke). She is preceded in death by her parents and a brother Steven.

Connie’s first love was music, and she looked for ways to be involved with music throughout her life. She learned to play the piano in her youth then added the flute and piccolo in junior high and high school. She was accomplished enough at the piano in her mid-teens to play hymns for church services. Later in life she learned to play instruments such as the harp, accordion, steel drums and ukulele. She shared her musical talents throughout her life in various ways: as the pianist for Community of Christ Church, as the organist for St. John’s Episcopal Church, and playing preludes and concerts at Grace Methodist Church and a Christmas concert at Bethel Baptist Church. She also accompanied her children’s orchestra class performances on the snare drum and other percussion instruments. She taught both her children how to read music and play the piano, and after they were grown and moved away from home, she started teaching piano lessons as another way to extend her love of music to others.

For family summer trips while Connie was growing up, they traveled in a van which her father had customized with a double bunk bed in place of the rear bench seat. Family trips included the Arches, Dinosaur National Monument, Yellowstone, Hole in the Rock and many others.

Connie was always at the top of her academic class. She had to work hard at times to maintain her A’s, but she really wanted to excel and succeed in her studies. She was always on the honor roll at school, and was one of the top students of her graduating high school class. Connie graduated from Dixie High School in Saint George UT. She received her degree of associate in science from Dixie College (now Southern Utah University). She also attended Utah State University.

After graduating from high school, Connie worked at Bryce Canyon National Park for the summer. It became one of her favorite places on earth and was one of the places she and Collin visited on their honeymoon.

During 1981-1982 Connie served a full-time mission for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in the England London East Mission.

Connie was introduced to Collin by a mutual friend, sometime during the summer of 1985. They started dating in the spring of 1986 and got engaged in early August of that year. They were married in the Saint George Utah temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on October 10, 1986.

Connie was a devoted mother to her two children and was intimately involved as a homeschool mom from the start of their education through high school. It brought her great satisfaction to watch her children learn and grow in knowledge, and she very much enjoyed learning along with them. She participated in local homeschool groups with her children and made many friends among homeschooling families. She and her family traveled to and camped at many of the national and state parks in New Mexico as part of the history and geography curriculum for her children.

She so much enjoyed being out in nature and was an avid hiker. She kept a record of the over 150 trails that she had hiked within the Sacramento Mountains. She and Collin began hiking together even before they were married. A most memorable hike was a 6-hour climb to the top of Mt. Nebo in Utah, where Collin proposed marriage to Connie.

From the time Connie was very young, each year the Anderson family would get together to celebrate Grandma Anderson’s birthday. That birthday celebration eventually turned into a regular family reunion where Connie enjoyed playing with her cousins and visiting with members of the Anderson family.
After she and Collin retired, they bought a motorhome and joined the Family RV Association. They enjoyed participating in the conventions and rallies organized by FRVA and made many new friends.

A life celebration will be held on Saturday, August 22, 2026, between 2 and 4 pm at The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, 1800 23rd St, Alamogordo NM. Family and friends are warmly invited for a time of fellowship and light refreshments as they share memories and celebrate Connie’s remarkable life.

Please arrange for any flowers to be delivered to 3100 Los Robles, Alamogordo, NM 88310.

item.title: Lady Alamogordo Tigers Soccer Split Games at Silver City Tournament
item.description:
Silver N.M.- The Alamogordo Lady Tigers had a mixed performance at the Silver City Tournament this weekend, securing a victory in their opening match before falling to Miyamura in a contest cut short by severe weather.

First Match Victory

Alamogordo dominated their opening matchup against Silver, claiming a 2-1 victory behind goals from London Curry and Zoey Spataro. Curry struck first to put the Lady Tigers ahead 1-0 at the 50-minute mark, with Spataro adding an insurance goal to seal the win.

“It was a solid opening performance,” said the team following the victory. Alamogordo moved to 1-0 in tournament play and was set to face Miyamura in their next contest.

Tournament Ends Early for Lady Tigers

The Lady Tigers’ tournament run came to an abrupt end in their second match when dangerous lightning forced officials to call the game with 25 minutes remaining. At that point, Miyamura had established a commanding 4-0 lead.

The match was suspended due to safety concerns for both teams and spectators as severe weather moved into the Silver City area.

Looking Ahead

The loss drops Alamogordo’s record to 1-1 overall. The Lady Tigers will look to bounce back with a home matchup against Deming scheduled for Tuesday. The team will have the opportunity to regroup and refocus before continuing their season.

Fans are encouraged to come out and support the Lady Tigers as they host Deming on Tuesday evening.

item.title: Sidney Paul Gordon Shooting Range Reports Strong July Performance; Second 100-Yard Bay Operational
item.description:
La Luz, New Mexico Reporting by Journalist Chris Edwards — The Sidney Paul Gordon Shooting Range is marking a significant expansion with the completion of its second 100-yard multipurpose bay and announcing preparations for two major regional championships in the coming weeks.

Facility Expansion Supports Growing Demand

The newly operational 100-yard bay represents a major capacity upgrade. Clean fill material has been delivered and spread across the impact berm and 40 feet along side berms, thanks to donations from local nonprofit organizations. The facility’s decision to construct 100-yard deep bays is already proving beneficial, providing ideal depths for diverse shooting events.

“This depth is ideal for so many different shooting events,” said Mark Douglas, Range Director.

Strong July Operations

The range safely served 816 people in July, including 69 participants in five competitions and events. This month’s activity reflects the facility’s growing importance as a regional shooting venue.

The range continues to support 10 different law enforcement agencies, including the Alamogordo Police Department, Otero County Sheriff’s Department, New Mexico State Police, U.S. Border Patrol, U.S. Air Force Office of Special Investigations, and several others.

Regional Championships Bring National Attention

This weekend, the USPSA Area 2 Steel Challenge Championship will draw competitors from Florida to California. Often described as “drag racing with a gun,” the event will utilize all eight General-Purpose bays. The 200-yard bay is being used for participant parking, while the 50-yard bay serves as a function test area. The Otero Practical Shooting Association is hosting and coordinating the competition.

Looking ahead, the range will host the USPSA Area 2 High Desert NM Sectional Championship during the third week of October. The event has already generated significant interest, with 250 registered participants and a waiting list. The new multipurpose bay was one of the key factors in bringing this prestigious championship back to the Sidney Paul Gordon Shooting Range.

Financial and Operational Update

July brought $7,738.87 in income from fees, target and snack sales, donations, passes, and taxes. The facility’s diverse revenue streams reflect its multi-purpose mission serving competitive shooters, law enforcement agencies, and recreational users.

In July, the range sold 57 passes of various categories, with notable demand from military discount holders (32 passes) and families seeking recreational access.

Community Connections

The report highlighted two touching moments. Staff discovered an abandoned briefcase at the front gate, which turned out to be a donation from a longtime customer who passed away in 2025—a high-quality metallic rifle rest that will serve future range users.

The facility also hosted some unexpected summer visitors: four baby skunks that took refuge under the classroom deck, obtaining water from the HVAC condensation line. The skunks behaved considerately, moving out within a few weeks.

Facility Improvements Continue

The range recently replaced two 25-year-old signs along South Scenic Drive, which serves as a popular walking and exercise area. The facility also coordinated mileage markers along Scenic Boulevard with the Friends of the Land and Legacy Recreation (FOLLR) organization, promoting both the shooting range and the outdoor recreation area.

Growing Digital Presence

The range’s online visibility continues expanding. Facebook generated 7,256 views in July, representing a 57 percent increase from July 2025. Google Business Profile interactions reached 41 calls (up 5.1% year-over-year), with 128 direction requests. Searches for “shooting range” and “shooting range near me” continue to drive discovery of the facility.

Looking Ahead

With two major USPSA championships on the calendar and continued facility improvements, the Sidney Paul Gordon Shooting Range is positioned as a premier regional venue for competitive and recreational shooting sports.

For information about range hours, fees, and upcoming events, visit the facility’s website or Facebook page.

item.title: PNM BILLING CRISIS DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - In what could be the most significant consumer protection crisis facing Alamogordo families in recent memory, Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) continues to impose unexplained billing increases of $100 to $300 per month on residents already struggling with the rising cost of living.

What makes the situation worse: some residents report bills showing usage three times higher than normal—a discrepancy PNM blames on short-staffed meter readers and estimated billing rather than actual usage readings.

Only one local political leader has publicly challenged these practices: Mayor Sharon McDonald, who directly contacted PNM leadership to express municipal concerns about the billing abuse.

Estimated Billing: The Hidden Problem

Dozens of Alamogordo residents report the same troubling pattern: their PNM electricity bills have skyrocketed due to estimated billing rather than actual meter readings.

"I'm an elderly woman on a fixed income," one affected resident shared. "My PNM bill jumped $280 one month. I didn't add any new appliances. I didn't change my usage. When I called PNM to ask why, they couldn't give me a straight answer other than that they're short-staffed in meter readers and may have estimated my usage."

This is the core of the problem: PNM is charging residents based on estimated usage rather than actual meter readings, and when residents call to verify the charges, they receive vague explanations about staffing shortages instead of concrete explanations or corrections.

Families are forced to choose between paying utility bills and purchasing groceries. Elderly residents on fixed incomes face the choice between staying cool in Alamogordo's summer heat and maintaining other basic necessities.

Mayor McDonald Takes Action

Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald has contacted PNM leadership directly to express the city's concerns regarding the systematic billing problems affecting residents. She made clear that these are not isolated customer service complaints—they represent a widespread pattern demanding corporate accountability.

"This is exactly what we should expect from elected leadership," consumer advocate and District 51 candidate Grace Nagamine said. "Mayor McDonald recognized that Alamogordo's families needed someone with a voice loud enough to reach corporate headquarters. She answered that call.

The question now is: where are the others?"

Nagamine Provides Action Plan for Residents

District 51  NM State Representative candidate Grace Nagamine has issued a comprehensive action plan providing Alamogordo residents with direct pathways to hold PNM accountable through official regulatory channels.

"This isn't about social media posts," Nagamine emphasized. "This is about making noise where it actually counts—with regulators and corporate leadership who have legal obligations to respond."

Residents can take action immediately:

FILE A COMPLAINT with the Public Regulation Commission at:

https://www.prc.nm.gov/consumer-relations/file-a-complaint/

Phone: (505) 827-4500 

SUBMIT A COMPLAINT to the New Mexico Attorney General at:

https://nmdoj.gov/get-help/submit-a-complaint/

Phone: (505) 827-6000 | Email: consumer@nmag.gov

SEND A CERTIFIED LETTER to PNM Corporate Headquarters:

One First Financial Center, Albuquerque, NM 87158

CALL PNM PUBLIC RELATIONS to formally document your complaint:

(505) 241-2700 (Business Hours, Monday-Friday)

The Silence from Other Political Leaders

As families face $100-$300 monthly billing increases from estimated usage, most of Alamogordo's political establishment has remained silent. City commissioners, county commissioners, and state representatives have offered no public statements, contacted no PNM leadership, and requested no regulatory investigations to date via any public statements. 

This is not a complex issue requiring expert analysis. Alamogordo families are being overcharged based on estimated usage. They cannot get explanations. They are suffering financial hardship.

Why Official Complaints Matter

The power to demand accountability rests with citizens, not political figures. Formal complaints to the Public Regulation Commission carry legal weight. Complaints to the Attorney General create an official record. Certified letters to corporate headquarters require documented response.

Social media posts change nothing. Official complaints to regulatory agencies change everything.

If enough residents file formal complaints, the Public Regulation Commission will be forced to investigate. If systematic overbilling is confirmed, PNM will face enforcement actions, penalties, and demands for customer remediation.

ACT NOW

Document your bills and usage patterns

File a complaint with the PRC online or by phone

Submit a complaint to the Attorney General's office

Send a certified letter to PNM Corporate demanding explanation

Call PNM Public Relations to formally document your complaint

Do not accept vague explanations. Do not allow PNM to hide behind customer service scripts. Make noise where it counts.

item.title: In Loving Memory of Ethel Mae (Seelye) Killebrew
item.description:
Ethel Mae (Seelye) Killebrew, age 84, entered the presence of her Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ, on July 31, 2026. She was born on February 28, 1942, in Muskegon, Michigan, to Betty and Leroy Seelye.

Ethel shared a beautiful marriage of 64 years with her beloved husband, Kenneth Killebrew. Together they built a life centered on faith, love, and family, creating a legacy that will continue for generations.

She was a devoted mother to her two sons, Jeff (Maritza) Killebrew and Mike (Laura) Killebrew. She was a proud and loving grandmother to Josh, Josiah, Alex (Jessica), Gabe (Myrna), Rebecca (Jon), Levi (Millie), Charles (Ally), and Paul, and a cherished great-grandmother to Anela, Oliver, Sawyer, Kora, Ayla, and Casen - oh, and don’t forget Buddy!
Ethel is also lovingly remembered by her sisters, Barbara Hoeker and Ruthie (Bud) Clark, and brothers, Earl and Roy Seelye, along with many extended family members and dear friends whose lives were enriched by her love and kindness.

Above all, Ethel was a woman of deep faith who loved everyone she met and found joy in serving others. Her family was her greatest joy, and she faithfully nurtured those she loved with a generous heart, gentle spirit, and steadfast example, touching countless lives with her compassionate heart. She leaves behind a legacy of faith, love, and grace that will continue to inspire all who knew her.

Though her family grieves her passing, they rejoice in the assurance that she is now at peace in the presence of her Savior. Her memory will forever be cherished until that joyful day when they are reunited in Christ.

A Celebration of Life for close family and friends will be held at 11a.m. on August 29, 2026, at Iglesia Triunfante Assembly of God church in Alamogordo, NM.

In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to St. Jude’s Children’s Hospital to help fight childhood cancer and other life-threatening diseases.

item.title: Alamogordo Public Schools Opens State-of-the-Art Holloman Middle School
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - A vision forged through partnership has become reality. On Thursday, Alamogordo Public Schools unveiled the brand-new Holloman Middle School, a $60 million architectural achievement that transforms education on Holloman Air Force Base and represents a bold commitment to military-connected students and families.

The new facility—designed by Dekker Design and constructed by Bradbury Stamm Construction—marks the completion of an innovative, fully integrated PreK-8 public school campus. It replaces aging structures that had served the base since 1973, introducing 21st-century learning spaces with higher-capacity classrooms, modern outdoor environments, and collaborative areas designed to optimize resources across the entire PreK-8 campus.

“When we broke ground on this spot, we shared a bold vision for what this campus could become,” said Michael Crabtree, Superintendent of Alamogordo Public Schools. “Standing here today, looking out at this state-of-the-art facility, I can proudly say that vision is now a reality. This project is a testament to the enduring partnership between Holloman Air Force Base, our district, and our entire community.”

The ribbon-cutting ceremony brought together military leadership, state representatives, educators, civic leaders, and families to celebrate not just a new building, but new possibilities—a facility poised to serve thousands of students for generations to come.

item.title: Tularosa Water Tank Reaches 22 Feet as Village Urges Continued Conservation Efforts
item.description:
Tularosa residents have made meaningful progress in the ongoing water crisis, with the village’s main water tank now reaching 22 feet, according to an update released this week. However, officials are cautioning against complacency, warning that overall water usage has begun to increase again despite active water restrictions.

The Village of Tularosa remains under mandatory water conservation measures, which prohibit all outdoor watering and restrict indoor use to essential activities only. While the rising tank level represents weeks of collective conservation efforts by the community, village personnel emphasized that more work remains before restrictions can be safely lifted.

“We have made some really good progress over the last several days, but it appears that our overall water usage is beginning to increase again,” the village stated in this week’s public notice. “We need everyone to keep conserving so we can continue building our levels and get closer to lifting these restrictions.”

Conservation Efforts Showing Results—But Usage Rising

The dual message—celebrating progress while warning of slipping discipline—suggests that some residents may be relaxing conservation habits as visible improvements appear on the horizon. Village officials attribute the recent uptick in usage to this psychological effect, commonly known as “conservation fatigue.”

To maintain momentum toward unrestricted water access, the village is reminding residents of critical conservation practices:

• Wash only necessary loads of laundry and ensure all loads are full capacity

• Reduce shower duration

• Eliminate unnecessary water use throughout the home and yard

• Continue the outdoor watering ban

“The best way we can get there is by continuing to work together and keeping our usage as low as possible right now,” village officials said.

A Community Working Toward Normalcy

Restrictions have tested the patience of Tularosa residents, particularly those managing yards, trees, and plants during the dry months. The inability to irrigate landscaping has raised concerns about vegetation health and property values. However, officials framed ongoing conservation as the fastest path back to normalcy.

“I know everyone is ready to get back to normal, including being able to water our yards, trees and plants,” the village acknowledged in their statement.

What’s Next

Village personnel did not specify the exact water level needed to safely lift restrictions, but indicated that continued coordination between residents and village staff will be essential. As the tank level creeps toward its target, every conservation decision will count.

Tularosa residents are urged to remain vigilant about water use and to remember that collective action has already yielded visible results. The village expressed gratitude for residents’ cooperation and patience, calling on the community to maintain its conservation commitment in the coming weeks.

“Every gallon we conserve helps our Village personnel get us closer to the levels we need to safely return to normal water use,” officials stated. “We’ve come a long way, but we aren’t quite there yet!”

item.title: TIMBERON PRECAUTIONARY BOIL WATER ADVISORY Continues thru 8-21-26
item.description:
Timberon N.M - BOIL YOUR WATER BEFORE USING -Due to E. Coli detected in special samples during line repairs

BOIL YOUR WATER BEFORE USING

Fecal coliform and E. Coli bacteria were found in the water supply on 8/14/2026. These bacteria can make you sick and are a particular concern for people with weakened immune systems.

Bacterial contamination can occur when increased run-off enters the drinking water source (for example, following heavy rains). It can also happen due to a break in the distribution system (pipes) or a failure in the water treatment process.

What should I do? What does this mean?

• DO NOT DRINK THE WATER WITHOUT BOILING IT FIRST.

Bring all water to a boil, let it boil for three minutes, and let it cool before using, or use bottled water. Boiled or bottled water should be used for drinking, making ice, brushing teeth, washing dishes, and food preparation until further notice. Boiling kills bacteria and other organisms in the water.

• Fecal coliforms and E. Coli are bacteria whose presence indicates that the water may be contaminated with human or animal wastes. Microbes in these wastes can cause diarrhea, cramps, nausea, headaches, or other symptoms. They may pose a special health risk for infants, young children, and people with severely compromised immune systems.

• The symptoms above are not caused only by organisms in drinking water. If you experience any of these symptoms and they persist, you may want to seek medical advice. People at increased risk should seek advice from their health care providers about drinking this water.

What is being done?

TWSD-Water System Operations Personnel conducted disinfection procedures 8/14/26-8/16/26. Microorganism sampling results for these efforts were received 8/17/26 and at this time indicate negative for Total Coliform and Fecal Coliform (E. Coli).

Timberon Water and Sanitation District is extending a boil water advisory to 8/21/26 to allow TWSD-Water System Personnel to continue monitoring the distribution system.

The public will be notified once their study is complete and the advisory has been removed.

item.title: Sunspot Update: Mercury Removed from Telescope, but a Different Spill Emerges
item.description:
Sunspot N.M. By Dave Dooling for Alamogordo Town News -Mercury has been removed from the Dunn Solar Telescope at Sunspot Solar Observatory, but the National Science Foundation is saying little else for the moment. Meanwhile, Alamogordo Town News has learned of an older, different kind of spill at Sunspot. And, subtle wording of Federal law allowed NSF to avoid reporting the mercury spill to a national database.

“Thank you for reaching out,” Cassandra Eichner, an NSF Media Affairs specialist, told Alamogordo Town News on Thursday in response to a multi-point inquiry. “The Mercury was safely removed from the telescope. NSF will issue a public update on Sacramento Peak Observatory later this month.”

Eichner ignored additional questions about mercury vapors coating surfaces and about plans to request proposals for a demolition contractor.

Meanwhile, a report of an older, different kind of hazardous leak at Sunspot appeared in a national database on July 6.

The new report claims that an unknown quantity of PCB (polychlorinated biphenyl) was spilled at Sunspot around 2016. The spill is reported in the 2026 database at the U.S. Coast Guard’s National Response Center (NRC), which is the “designated federal point of contact for reporting all oil, chemical, radiological, biological and etiological discharges into the environment, as well as railroad incidents, anywhere in the United States and its territories.”

The July 6 entry reads: “Caller reporting an old mineral oil (PCB) spill at the Sunspot Observatory. This spill is reported to have taken place around 20 years ago, but was never cleaned up. Caller states they have been told which shaft and which location the spill is at. Caller states the observatory is closing down, and they believe the spill will be covered up.” No other detail is available.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), PCBs had uses ranging from carbonless copy paper to electrical transformers between 1929 and their international ban in 1979 due to a range of adverse health effects, including cancer. Because they were widely used as an insulator in transformers, many sources remain in use.

The threshold, or minimum reporting quantity (Final RQ), set by Federal law for both PCB and mercury is one pound (0.454 kg). Information should first go to the National Response Center, which “fields INITIAL reports for pollution and railroad incidents and forwards that information to appropriate federal/state agencies for response.”

Reports from 1990 forward are available online as spreadsheets. A search from 2000 to today — covering “about 20 years ago”— has no other mention of Sunspot. How the spill is cleaned up will depend on the source, extent, and location. Cleanups often involve removing contaminated soil to safe disposal sites. EPA recommended contacting the New Mexico Environment Department with regard to handling the PCB spill. ATN found nothing in their on-line records and has submitted a query.

To be certain a report of a mercury leak at Sunspot was not overlooked, ATN filed a request with the NRC. On May 21, it replied, “Unfortunately, we were unable to find any NRC report regarding your request about a mercury spill at Sunspot.”

A subtlety in the wording of Federal law — 40 CFR, Part 302, Designation, Reportable Quantities, and Notification — allowed NSF to avoid reporting the spill. It defines a release as “any spilling, leaking, … into the environment.” The last three words are critical. The cleanup contract clearly described the leak as staying within the building.

EPA confirmed that “that releases of hazardous substances that are contained entirely within a facility and that do not enter the environment [including ambient air] are not required to be reported” under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA).

But NSF’s silence following the initial announcement led to public speculation ranging to the sensational, including a large puddle sitting outside the Dunn, ready to roll downhill to Alamogordo.

The reality was simpler: only 186 pounds (about 1.6 gallon) leaked, although another 18,000 pounds (160 gallons) remained in the bearings and could have been released without proper control, which now has been done.

An additional factor emerged in other discussions with Alamogordo Town News, an effect called adsorption. This means vapors adhere to surfaces, not absorption, meaning soaking into a material. A 1982 study at the University of Auckland, New Zealand, showed that painted surfaces and vinyl flooring — both present in the Dunn — adsorb vapors like mercury. Because this is a surface effect, the bond is weak and surfaces can just as easily release vapors to the environment.

But, EPA case studies also show that mercury can be removed from a facility, which can then return to normal operation. The most serious case, at a home in Las Vegas, involved a 17-year-old boy smearing a quart of mercury (1/6 the amount released at Sunspot) around his grandmother’s house and poisoning himself. Yet, after removing hazardous material equivalent to a 13-foot cube and coating some surfaces with epoxy, the house was remediated and the owner was allowed to return.

The statement by NSF’s Eichner that “Mercury was safely removed” implies that surfaces inside the Dunn have been assessed as mercury-free or cleaned where they had adsorbed vapors. 

Otherwise, the planned demolition could release mercury into ambient air, as specified under the Comprehensive Response Act. And this returns to an earlier question about the Dunn: If the mercury is gone, what public health hazard remains? Why rush to demolish?

About the journalist: Dave Dooling is a veteran areospace writer and educator who lives in High Rolls New Mexico. He recently retired as education director at the New Mexico Museum of Spac history, and now runs The Traveling Gizmo Show.

item.title: Alamogordo Town News Investigative Report: PNM’s Alleged Over Billing Scheme Exposed, Overcharging Residents by the Thousands
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - An investigation by 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News has uncovered evidence of an alleged systematic over-billing by Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) affecting customers across the Alamogordo region. Multiple residents have reported improper rate-tier charges following the utility’s July 2026 billing disruptions, revealing a pattern that regulators say could potentially represent hundreds of thousands of dollars in overcharges.

This is not an isolated case.

Over the past two weeks, our newsroom has received complaints from dozens of households in Alamogordo and Ruidoso reporting nearly identical billing anomalies—all stemming from the same period when PNM failed to conduct timely meter readings due to staffing shortages. The excuse given by the PNM call center staff is that the area had staffing shortages with meter readers and that they say estimated many  people’s bills. 

This is not an isolated billing error.

Over the past two weeks, our newsroom has received complaints from multiple households in Alamogordo, Ruidoso, and surrounding areas reporting nearly identical improper charges, all stemming from PNM's July 2026 billing disruption period.

PNM confirmed that it operates 8,764 meters across the Alamogordo and Ruidoso areas.

 If even a portion experienced the same over billing pattern documented in this investigation, customers in this region alone have been overcharged by hundreds of thousands of dollars.

To understand how PNM may have systematically overbilled customers, we analyzed an actual bill from an Alamogordo resident and cross-referenced it against PNM's own published rate schedule which shows the discrepancy. 

This is a straightforward, normal amount of residential electricity usage for a two-month summer billing period in southern New Mexico.

PNM's tiered rate structure (Residential Rate 1A) clearly shows three pricing blocks:

This tiered structure is designed to encourage conservation—the more electricity you use, the higher rate you pay on incremental usage.

Instead of calculating charges across two separate billing periods, PNM consolidated all 2,397 kWh into a single bill and applied rates as follows:

According to PNM's own tariff requirement, stated in their response to regulators:

"If your bill includes more than one month of service, your energy usage will be spread across the applicable billing months before charges are calculated."

When properly split across two 30-day billing periods, the same 2,397 kWh should have been charged as follows:

The overcharge mechanism is elegant in its deception:

By consolidating two months of normal usage into a single billing statement, PNM artificially pushed 537 kilowatt-hours into Block 3 pricing territory when, under normal billing procedures, the customer would never have reached Block 3.

Here's the critical difference:

The customer was charged the highest tier rate for electricity they used across two normal billing months. Under proper billing, those same kWh would have been charged entirely at Block 1 and Block 2 rates.

The $107.11 Block 3 charge is the core of the overcharge. Additionally, customers were charged $138.25 for 930 kWh in Block 2 when, if usage had been properly distributed, only $79.84 in Block 2 charges should have applied across both months.

When we began investigating this case, we contacted multiple residents who had filed complaints about July-August 2026 bills. The consistency was striking:

"They kept saying the bill was correct because I used the power," one resident told us. "I did use the power—over two months. But they charged me as if I used it all in one month at premium rates."

"When I showed them my math, they offered to split it into two payments. They didn't fix it. They just made the overbilling more convenient for me to pay," said another.

PNM's own disclosure reveals the scope:

Up to 8,764 meters in Alamogordo and Ruidoso areas could have been affected by delayed or estimated billing during the July 2026 disruption in staffing.

Conservative estimates of the impact

In the Alamogordo and Ruidoso areas alone, customers may have been overcharged by $130,000 to over $500,000 if the scenario above is widespread.

If similar practices occurred across PNM's broader New Mexico service territories during this billing disruption period, the statewide total could easily exceed $1-2 million in customer overbilling.

When the complaint was escalated to the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (PRC), PNM's written response promised what it had already failed to deliver.

"If your bill includes more than one month of service, your energy usage will be spread across the applicable billing months before charges are calculated. This helps ensure you are not billed as though all usage occurred in a single month."

Rather than recalculate charges with properly distributed usage, PNM offered only to split the inflated bill into two equal payments of approximately $240 each in the example scenario above and similar accounts as per other customers we have spoke to. 

This is not a correction. This is not a refund. This is asking the customer to pay the inflated amount on a convenient payment plan.

"It's as if someone overcharged you $58 on a bill, and when you complained, they offered to let you pay it in two installments. The problem isn't solved—it's just deferred,"said one regulatory analyst.

The timing of PNM's overbilling raises red flags for regulators and consumer advocates.

PNM is currently in acquisition negotiations. The utility is being evaluated as a potential acquisition target by larger utility company and the acquisition has been under regulatory scrutiny. During these negotiations, and review by regulators and legislators PNM's financial statements, revenue reports, and profitability metrics are under intense scrutiny.

Systematically overbilling thousands of customers during this exact window could potentially:

"If there's systematic overbilling occurring during an acquisition evaluation period, that's material information," said one utility industry observer and consumer advocate. "It could potentially mean the company's reported financial performance may not reflect actual, sustainable earnings. It raises questions on whether this is a one off issue or potentially a sustained practice of over-billing.  Customers may have been inflating the company's revenue to benefit acquisition bidders if this issue is widespread or has existed not as an isolated case.”

The coincidence—that meter reading failures, billing consolidation errors, and improper rate tiering all occurred simultaneously during the company's sensitive period of trying to close an acquisition —raises questions about whether this was negligence, systemic failure, or something more deliberate. Time, investigations and transparency will tell rather this was isolated or systematic. 

The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission has formally documented complaints filed by multiple Alamogordo and Ruidoso residents. Commission staff are examining PNM's billing methodology during the affected period and are allegedly requesting documentation on how the utility calculated charges for consolidated multi-month bills. Alamogordo Town News has asked for details of any investigations and is filing an IPRA for more details. 

The New Mexico Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division has also been notified and is allegedly reviewing the matter, Alamogordo Town News is seeking more information. 

Both agencies have broad authority to:

If systematic overbilling is substantiated, isolated and or widespread the Attorney General could pursue additional remedies under consumer fraud and unfair business practices statutes.

Utility billing experts we consulted were unanimous in their assessment:

"This is a clear tariff violation," said one regulatory analyst with 20 years of utility oversight experience. "PNM's own rules require that multi-month bills have usage spread across the appropriate billing periods for rate calculation. The company did the opposite—it consolidated usage to push customers into higher tiers. That's not a clerical error; that's a structural problem."

"When you consolidate two months of normal usage into one bill, you're essentially gaming the rate structure. The tiered system is designed to charge different rates based on monthly consumption patterns. By combining months, you destroy that design and artificially inflate rates. Every customer affected should receive a refund," observed another expert.

A third observer focused on the timing: "The coincidence of this overbilling occurring during acquisition negotiations and regulatory review is troubling. Regulators need to ask whether this was a deliberate revenue-boost strategy or a systemic failure. Either answer is problematic."

As the NMPRC and the Attorney General's office begin their investigations, a central question emerges:

Was this an isolated software error affecting a few hundred customers, or does it represent a systematic practice that affected thousands?

And more troublingly: Did PNM benefit financially from this overbilling during a period when its acquisition value was being determined?

The answers will determine whether this becomes a modest billing correction or a major consumer protection scandal.

If you received a PNM bill in July or August 2026 that included more than one month of service, or if your bill showed unusually high charges in Block 2 or Block 3 rates, you may have been overbilled.

File a formal complaint at:www.prc.nm.gov

Or  call: (505) 827-7500

item.title: Alamogordo Town News Special Report: Why Your PNM Bill is So High This Month?
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - Delayed meter reads left many of Alamogordo and Ruidoso households with a single bill covering two months of summer power. Here is what happened, how the rate tiers actually work, and what you can do about it.

To many households across Alamogordo, Ruidoso, and Tularosa opened their mailboxes this month to a Public Service Company of New Mexico bill roughly twice the size of anything they had seen before. Some totals ran past $450 for customers accustomed to paying in the low $200s.

The cause was not a rate hike buried in the fine print, and it was not a metering error. It was a staffing shortage in PNM's meter reading operation that pushed bills off schedule and, for many customers, folded two months of the hottest weather of the year into one statement with some meter readings estimated.

PNM says 8,764 meters are in the area with many placed on estimated or delayed billing after the company began estimating reads on July 21. The utility notified customers of the problem on August 3, roughly two weeks after estimation began, and says the staffing shortages have since been resolved.

For households on tight monthly budgets, the arithmetic of a combined bill is punishing regardless of whether it is calculated correctly. A bill that should have arrived as two payments of about $240 instead arrived as one demand for $477.

Much of the confusion and anger circulating locally stems from a genuine misunderstanding of PNM's tiered pricing.

It is worth walking through carefully, because the structure is not intuitive and PNM's bill does very little to explain it.

Residential customers on Rate 1A are billed in three blocks, with the price per kilowatt-hour climbing as usage rises:

Block 3 power costs more than twice what Block 1 power costs. The structure is deliberate: it is designed to reward conservation and penalize heavy consumption.

This proration is the mechanism PNM referred to when it told state regulators that on a multi-month bill, "your energy usage will be spread across the applicable billing months before charges are calculated.

The wording is accurate but nearly opaque to anyone who is not a rate analyst, and it appears nowhere in plain language on the bill itself.

One Alamogordo household provided its August statement for this article. The meter was read on August 10 covering 62 days and 2,397 kWh — an average of 38.7 kWh per day, consistent with running air conditioning through a record-hot summer.

Because the billing period ran 62 days, each block allowance was doubled:

This is the question nearly every affected customer is asking. We ran it both ways.

Split into two 31-day periods at 1,198.5 kWh each, each month would have been allotted 465 kWh in Block 1 and 465 kWh in Block 2, with the remaining 268.5 kWh landing in Block 3.

Though there is sticker shock by a combined bill it is actually $23.86 lower 

For moderate users, day-based proration is genuinely protective. A household averaging 23 kWh per day — about 700 kWh in a normal month — would use roughly 1,400 kWh over 62 days. Under a fixed 900 kWh ceiling, 500 kWh would have been dumped into the most expensive tier. With proration, that household stays entirely in Blocks 1 and 2 and pays nothing at the Block 3 rate.

The customers hit hardest by combined bills are the heaviest users, who were already in Block 3 every summer month and now see two months of it at once.

Several pressures landed simultaneously this summer, and the delayed bill concentrated all of them into one envelope.

The charges on these bills appear to be correctly calculated under the tariff on file with state regulators. That does not make the episode a non-story.

PNM's meter reading operation failed for a period of weeks, and the resulting cash-flow shock was absorbed entirely by customers. A household that budgets $240 a month for power does not have $477 available on demand simply because the arithmetic is defensible.

The communication failure compounded it. The bill shows "930.000" next to Block 1 with no indication anywhere on the statement that the figure represents 15 kWh per day across 62 days. A customer who knows the standard allowance is 450 kWh sees a number they cannot reconcile and reasonably concludes something is wrong. That confusion has driven a wave of local speculation about deliberate overcharging.

PNM could have prevented nearly all of it with one line of plain text on the affected bills explaining that block limits were doubled for the extended period. It did not.

Alamogordo Town News is continuing to report on this and is seeking answers on several points. We have been in contact with the leadership of PNM to get clarity and bring accurate information to consumers from PNM leaders. We will have a follow- up statement from PNM on Tuesday afternoon regarding…

If your PNM bill covered more than one month, or if you received an estimated read you believe was inaccurate contact PNM. 

Methodology: Block thresholds and the 15 kWh per day proration were verified against PNM's published Rate 1A tariff and the company's own bill definitions, which state that the first two blocks are billed up to 450 kWh each with the third block covering usage above 900 kWh. Charges were recalculated independently from an actual customer statement. Usage and rate figures come directly from that bill. PNM's account of the staffing shortage, the estimation start date, and the 8,764 affected meters comes from the company's written response to the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission.

Correction: An earlier version of this report that was not yet validated was published but not pushed for wide release for 3 hours in error, and stated that PNM had improperly shifted usage into higher rate tiers by combining two billing periods. That was incorrect. PNM prorates block allowances by the number of days billed, and the charges reviewed were consistent with the filed tariff. Alamogordo Town News regrets the error, as soon as the error was confirmed, the story was corrected as per above. We regret and apologize for any error in our understanding of the tier 1 limits.

item.title: In Memory of Eva Marie Arone (Linehan)
item.description:
With profound sadness and deep love, we announce the passing of Eva Marie Arone (Linehan), age 61, of Alamogordo, New Mexico, on August 11, 2026.

Eva was born on September 1, 1964, in Rantoul, Illinois. As the daughter of an Air Force airman, she spent her early years living in several Air Force Base locations throughout the country, before her family came to Holloman Air Force Base in 1972. The following year, they settled in Alamogordo, a community that Eva would call home for the rest of her life and to which she would devote her talents, energy, and heart.

Eva attended North Elementary School for fourth, fifth, and sixth grades, Chaparral Junior High School, Alamogordo Mid High School, and graduated from Alamogordo Senior High School in 1982. After graduation, she attended local college classes and began working in Alamogordo, eventually discovering a career that would become her lifelong passion in the printing industry.

As the youngest of five children, Eva was deeply cherished by her family. Yet despite being the youngest, she was often the one who stepped forward when her family needed her most. Throughout her life, she provided unwavering support to her siblings and especially to her mother, Barbara, whose presence remained a source of comfort, friendship, and strength.

Eva's love for family was evident in both her words and her actions. When she and Rick built their dream home on South Canyon Road, there was never any question that it would include a place for her mother. Eva lovingly ensured that an apartment was part of the plan, creating a home where her mother, whom she considered both a parent and one of her very best friends, would always be welcome. It was a reflection of Eva's generous heart and her belief that family should remain close, connected, and cared for throughout life's journey.

Family was at the center of Eva's life, and nowhere was that more evident than in her enduring love story with her husband, Richard "Rick" Arone. The two found each other in the mid-1980s and quickly formed a bond that would last a lifetime. Together for nearly forty years and married for almost thirty, Eva and Rick built a life grounded in love, friendship, loyalty, and laughter. They often shared the story of how they cemented their romance and commitment to one another on the dance floor of the old Desperado Bar and Dance Hall, where their journey together truly began.

Rick was a loving and steadfast partner who stood beside Eva through life's joys, challenges, and periods of illness. Their relationship was built on a foundation of mutual respect, devotion, and unwavering commitment. No matter the circumstances, Rick remained a constant source of strength, comfort, and support. Whenever the subject of her marriage arose, Eva was quick to say that Rick was "a good man and a loving husband." Those simple words reflected the deep appreciation and gratitude she felt for the life they built together. The bond they shared was one of Eva's greatest treasures and a source of strength throughout her life.

After several years working in the printing industry, Eva joined forces with her colleague, trusted friend, and self-described "partner in crime," Mike Cross, to pursue their dream of owning a business together. In 2002, they opened A C Print & Design on White Sands Boulevard.

Built on hard work, determination, and an unwavering belief in the importance of serving the local community, A C Print quickly earned a reputation for quality, reliability, and outstanding customer service. The business became a trusted partner for local organizations, schools, businesses, nonprofits, and community events throughout Alamogordo and Otero County.

Eva and Mike were passionate about A C Print and dedicated themselves wholeheartedly to its success. Together they invested countless hours, often working long days, late nights, and weekends to ensure the business thrived. Their commitment required personal sacrifices, but they never lost sight of their goal: creating a successful local business that would support their families, serve their customers, and contribute to the well-being of the Alamogordo community they loved.

Through their leadership and dedication, A C Print became one of Alamogordo's most respected small businesses and was recognized multiple times by the Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce for outstanding business achievement. For Eva, however, the greatest reward was not the recognition but the relationships she built and the opportunity to help others succeed through the work she loved. The success of A C Print stands as a testament to the vision, determination, and community spirit that Eva and Mike shared.

Eva was admired for her strength, generosity, creativity, determination, and unwavering commitment to those she loved. She made lasting friendships wherever she went and touched countless lives through both her professional accomplishments and her caring spirit. Her kindness, warm smile, and willingness to help others created a lasting impact on all who knew her.

She is survived by her beloved husband, Richard "Rick" Arone; her brothers, David Linehan and Patrick Linehan; and many extended family members, friends, colleagues, and community members who will cherish her memory.

Eva was preceded in death by her mother, Barbara Eppler Linehan; her brother, Danny Linehan; her sister, Theresa Linehan; and her longtime friend, business partner, and trusted confidant, Mike Cross. Together, Eva and Mike built not only a successful business but also a lasting legacy of service to the Alamogordo community.

Though our hearts are heavy with loss, we take comfort in the many memories Eva leaves behind and the enduring legacy she created through her family, her friendships, her business, and her devotion to her community. She will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing her.

"A life measured not only by accomplishments, but by the kindness shared, the friendships formed, and the lives touched along the way."

item.title: Albertsons Issues Massive Recall of 59 Products Over Salmonella Risk
item.description:
Albertsons Issues Massive Recall of 59 Products Over Salmonella Risk

Albertsons has recalled 59 store-made items available for purchase in New Mexico stores due to the risk of salmonella contamination, marking a significant food safety concern for the region.

The Source of the Problem

The voluntary recall was initiated after a supplier called Ron’s Home Style Foods recalled products, with the affected items containing pico de gallo made with jalapeños that were recalled in association with an ongoing FDA investigation involving Coast Citrus Distributors. The recall has ties to a major outbreak involving jalapeños available at Chipotle.

What’s Being Recalled

The recalled products span a wide range of prepared foods sold at store delis and prepared meals sections. The items were available for purchase at Albertsons Market, Market Street, Amigos and United stores in New Mexico and Texas.

Among the recalled products are smoked brisket nachos, pizzas, quesadillas, enchiladas, breakfast items, catering platters, and fresh guacamole. All products have specific sell-through dates ranging from mid-July through mid-August 2026.

What Customers Should Do

If you purchased any of these items, the company is urging you not to consume them. Instead, you should throw it away or return it for a full refund.

For questions about the recall, Albertsons has established a customer service center. Albertsons has a customer service center open Monday through Friday, 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. MT, for any questions.

item.title: PNM Answers Some Questions, But Alamogordo Citizens Seek More Clarity from Planned Thursday Meeting
item.description:
Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) will host a community outreach event this Thursday, August 20th, from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the Inkwell Innovation Center, offering customers a chance to get direct answers about the billing crisis that left thousands facing unexpectedly high electricity charges.

The company has released answers to several key questions about the situation, but frustration continues to mount among residents who experienced dramatic increases in their bills. Tularosa’s Mayor claims her electricity bill skyrocketed from a few hundred dollars to well over a thousand dollars—a story echoed by other affected customers across Alamogordo and surrounding communities.

What Went Wrong

The billing problems stemmed from an unexpected staffing shortage at PNM in July. According to the company, several meter readers left within a few weeks, leaving the Ruidoso, Alamogordo, and Tularosa area with just one meter reader by July 10th. Rather than have customers wait for actual meter readings, PNM began using estimated readings based on previous usage patterns.

PNM brought in trained employees from other parts of the state to stabilize operations while filling the open positions, which the company says were completed by the first week of August.

The Delayed Communication Problem

PNM acknowledges a critical communication failure. Notifications to customers came roughly two weeks after estimations began.

“While we were working through all the steps on our end, we missed an opportunity to communicate early and often,” the company stated in its response to customers.

The staffing shortage affected thousands: 8,047 customers in Alamogordo received multi-month bills, with 8,764 affected accounts total in the region.

What PNM Says Now

In response to customer concerns, PNM has provided the following information:

On billing accuracy: PNM states that once actual meter readings resumed, its billing system automatically adjusted any differences between estimated and actual usage. Customers should only be charged for electricity they actually used, the company says.

On explanations: Affected customers received direct communications explaining how block rate calculations were applied to their bills. However, PNM acknowledges that information may not have been clear enough for all customers.

On staffing: All vacant meter reader positions have been filled, and PNM says it does not expect any more billing delays or estimated meter reads due to staffing shortages in this area.

Questions Remain

While PNM has addressed several inquiries, many residents remain concerned about the accuracy of their bills and the methodology behind the estimates. The company’s explanation of block proration—the method used to calculate charges during the multi-month billing periods—continues to be a point of confusion for some customers.

Attend Thursday’s Event

PNM representatives will be at the Inkwell Innovation Center on Thursday, August 20th, from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. to speak directly with customers. Those with questions about their bills or concerns about the billing methodology are urged to attend.

Customers can also visit PNM’s payment center during regular business hours for assistance.

For more information, contact PNM Corporate Communications at 505-241-2794 or Eric.Chavez2@txnmenergy.com.

item.title: Why Budget, Policy, and Direction Must Come Before the City Manager
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M - by Dr. Stephanie Hernandez:

At my final meeting on June 9, I said what I believe should be the priority of the Commission and, ultimately, the citizens of Alamogordo: first the budget, second policy and direction, and third the city manager. Since then, I have been asked by employees and many citizens why I believe that order makes sense.

In my simple way of thinking, after seven years of service, much of the instability the City has experienced can be traced back to one recurring problem: too much focus on the city manager and not enough focus on the systems the city manager is meant to carry out. When the individual becomes the priority instead of the structure, the result can be turnover, inconsistency, and a loss of momentum.

That is why I believe the priorities should be clear: budget first, policy and direction second, and the city manager third. This does not diminish the role of the city manager. It puts the role where it belongs in a commission-manager form of government.

The Structure Matters

The City of Alamogordo operates under a commission-manager form of government. Under the City Charter, the Commission is the governing body and the city manager is the chief administrative officer. The Charter assigns the manager responsibility for carrying out ordinances and policies, managing employees, preparing the budget, and making recommendations concerning the welfare of the City. In other words, the manager is responsible for implementation, not for replacing the policy role of the Commission (City of Alamogordo, 2019; N.M. Stat. Ann. § 3-14-14).

That structure is important because the Commission is elected by the citizens to represent the public’s interests, priorities, and vision for the community. The city manager, as the sole employee of the governing body, is then responsible for turning that collective direction into administration and operations.

Diagram 1. Proper Chain of Accountability

This chain works best when information flows in both directions. Departments provide operational realities and needs to the city manager. The city manager presents the whole picture to the Commission. The Commission sets priorities on behalf of the citizens. Citizens, in turn, elect the Commission and hold it accountable.

1. Budget: The Story of the City

The budget should come first because without the money, nothing else matters. A municipal budget is not just a spreadsheet. It tells the story of where a city is, what it values, what it has neglected, and where it is trying to go.

There is a common saying: follow the money. Yet in local government, there is often very little sustained engagement with the budget beyond the formal adoption. That is a mistake. The budget should not be viewed only once a year and then forgotten. It is a living, breathing document that changes through the year as revenues fluctuate, projects shift, staffing changes, emergencies happen, and costs increase.

A city manager’s job is to prepare the budget and ensure it reflects both the needs of the departments and the direction of the Commission. The boots-on-the-ground input from departments is crucial because departments understand their operational realities. Public Works knows the condition of streets and drainage. Utilities know when lines and equipment are failing. Police and fire know what is needed to protect public safety. Community development knows where growth barriers exist. Quality-of-life departments understand the amenities that help residents stay and newcomers choose to move here.

Even so, each department naturally sees its own piece. The city manager must see the whole picture and combine all of those needs with the Commission’s vision to prepare a balanced and realistic budget. That is why the budget becomes the place where public priorities, operational realities, and financial limitations meet.

2. Policy and Direction: Ensuring the Future

If the budget tells the story of where the City is now, policy and direction determine where the City is going. This is the part of government that protects the future.

The Commission’s vision should not be only the individual vision of one or two commissioners. It should reflect the needs and priorities of their constituents. That is how the governing body ensures that City resources are working in the best interests of the citizens.

Policy is expressed through ordinances, resolutions, master plans, strategic plans, and other formally adopted actions. These should be reviewed regularly. An ordinance adopted decades ago may still be relevant, but it may also no longer reflect community needs, legal changes, or operational realities. Likewise, master plans should not gather dust on a shelf. They should guide growth, infrastructure, and service delivery over time.

Ordinances and resolutions serve different purposes. Generally, an ordinance creates or amends local law and has ongoing legal effect. A resolution usually expresses a policy position, approval, direction, or administrative decision of the governing body. New Mexico law recognizes the power of municipalities to adopt ordinances and requires certain procedures for proposed ordinances, including public notice requirements in many cases (N.M. Stat. Ann. §§ 3-17-1, 3-17-3, 3-17-4).

3. The City Manager: Implementing the Plan

The city manager should be the third priority because the role is to implement the Commission’s collective policy and budget through day-to-day administration. That includes personnel, legal compliance, contracts, purchasing, project coordination, operations, and countless routine decisions that keep the City functioning.

The manager must make decisions within the constraints of the adopted budget and the direction established by the governing body as a whole. The governing body is the collective boss. In Alamogordo, the mayor and commissioners share equal voting power except where otherwise provided by law or the Charter (City of Alamogordo, 2019).

That means no individual member of the dais should be treated as if he or she alone directs administration. Individual commissioners can and should raise ideas, unique projects, and constituent concerns. But once funding, staff time, or operational changes are involved, direction should be given collectively. If there is disagreement, it should be taken to the dais and resolved through public discussion and a vote, not politicized against the city manager for implementing the Commission’s adopted direction.

When the structure works as intended, there should be far fewer personalized controversies. The debate should be about policy, priorities, and funding, not about whether the city manager should be blamed for carrying out the policy direction of the governing body.

A Simple Example of How the Structure Should Work

Consider one example: the community wants to move toward a no-kill shelter.

1. 1. Identify the issue. Citizens, volunteers, and staff express the need for a no-kill shelter and bring the concern to the Commission.

2. 2. Create policy and direction. If a majority of the Commission agrees, the governing body can begin setting policy. That may include an ordinance adjusting fees to discourage irresponsible owner surrenders while reducing barriers for responsible owners. It may also include a resolution declaring the City’s direction to move toward a no-kill model.

3. 3. Give the city manager a roadmap. Once the governing body has spoken, the city manager can work with staff on how to make it happen. That may include free spay and neuter programs, free microchipping, more adoption events, rescue partnerships, public education, and the long-term goal of a larger or improved shelter.

4. 4. Balance it with other priorities. The city manager must then balance that work with all other city responsibilities and available funding. If the full goal cannot be accomplished in a single fiscal year, the City can phase the work over time while continuing progress in the direction approved by the Commission.

That same process should occur across all departments. Some priorities may move faster than others depending on cost and urgency, but every department should fit into a larger, continuous balancing act.

Diagram 2. Every Department Matters

Though core services such as water, sewer, public safety, and roads are critical, quality of life is what helps people want to live, stay, work, and invest here. Public safety, utilities, public works, community development, quality of life, and administration all depend on each other. If one area is ignored too long, the whole system suffers.

What Thriving Cities Often Have in Common

Cities that thrive often have two things in common: a clear vision for the future and consistency in leadership long enough to carry that vision forward. That does not mean a city manager alone makes a city successful. It means the structure stays focused long enough for good ideas to become results.

Examples from the Southwest show how this can work. Rio Rancho, New Mexico has used long-range planning and sustainability planning to connect vision, infrastructure, services, and growth. Las Cruces, New Mexico explicitly ties city-manager administration to mayor and council direction and uses strategic planning to align operations with community goals. Mesa, Arizona pairs council priorities with financial policies, annual balanced budgeting, and performance planning across departments. These cities differ in size, but they demonstrate the value of clear direction, disciplined budgeting, and administrative continuity.

The lesson for Alamogordo is not that we should copy another city line for line. The lesson is that communities are more likely to grow and prosper when they know where they are going and keep their attention on the system, not just on the person serving as city manager.

Why This Matters for Alamogordo

Alamogordo cannot rely forever on asking the same residents to shoulder more of the burden. For a city funded heavily through consumption-based revenues, higher prices alone are not the same thing as real expansion of the local tax base. Inflation can make revenues rise in dollars without producing stronger underlying growth.

That is why smart, steady growth matters. We need people to come live here and work here in every industry. We need housing, business investment, quality infrastructure, and quality-of-life amenities that help families choose Alamogordo and help existing residents remain here. Though we must focus on critical services, quality of life is also essential because it is part of what makes people want to live, stay, and move here.

Researching the past seven years only reinforced that conclusion for me: if Alamogordo wants to become one of the more prosperous and stable communities in the region, then the City must focus on budget discipline, clear policy direction, and consistent implementation. That is how we create an environment where growth can happen thoughtfully rather than accidentally.

Conclusion

So when I said at my final meeting that the priorities should be budget, policy and direction, and then the city manager, I meant exactly that.

The budget tells the story of where the City is and what it can afford to do. Policy and direction establish where the City is going. The city manager then takes those decisions and turns them into administration, operations, and results.

When those priorities are kept in the right order, decisions align better, public discussion becomes more meaningful, and leadership becomes more stable. The governing body can stay focused on representing the citizens, and the city manager can stay focused on carrying out the work. That is not just good governance. It is the best path toward building a stronger Alamogordo for today and for the next generation.

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez was born and raised in Alamogordo and returned home to serve the community that shaped her. She earned six degrees from NMSU, including a Ph.D. in Education, Leadership and Administration, along with master’s and bachelor’s degrees in economics, accounting, and related fields. After 20 years at NMSU (13 with the Foundation) building expertise in finance, accounting, and organizational leadership, she brought that experience to municipal leadership and public service in Alamogordo as Director of Finance, Assistant City Manager and a combined 27 month tenure as Acting City Manager..She is the spouse of retired Army veteran Cruz, a mother of three and grandmother of two, and currently teaches economics and finance.

item.title: In Memory of Betty Jean Vreeke-Skidmore
item.description:
Betty Jean Vreeke-Skidmore, 91, of Alamogordo, New Mexico, passed away peacefully in her sleep at home on August 13, 2026. Born November 23, 1934, in Lapeer, Michigan, she was the daughter of Hungarian immigrants John and Lydia Nagy.

Betty was predeceased by her parents; twelve brothers and sisters; and her husbands, Wayne Caldwell, Lynn Vreeke, and Bacil Skidmore. She is survived by eight stepdaughters, one stepson, one legally adopted son, numerous grandchildren, great‑grandchildren, and one great‑great‑grandchild, as well as many nieces, nephews, and extended family members.

Betty became a resident of Alamogordo in 1968 after traveling extensively throughout the United States and abroad. She worked in several positions over the years, including as a teller at Security Bank & Trust and as a cashier at Dill’s Meat Market, where she met her second husband, Lynn Vreeke. Later, becoming the night clerk at at the former Days Inn. During her marriage to Lynn, she served as pianist, treasurer, and board member of Eternity Baptist Church, contributing the remaining funds needed to complete the church building now located at 1205 25th Street. After Lynn’s passing, she later married Bacil Skidmore, a retired Army veteran.

In her senior years, Betty divided her time between Florida in the winter and Alamogordo in the summer, continuing her lifelong love of travel and adventure.

Funeral services were held Tuesday, August 18, at Scenic Chapel in Alamogordo. She will be laid to rest beside her second husband, Lynn Vreeke, at Monte Vista Cemetery, 1590 E. 1st Street, Alamogordo,NM. Pastor Fred McCloskey, of Eternity Baptist Church, will officiated the graveside service.

Betty lived a full, adventurous, and faith‑centered life. Her legacy endures in the many lives she touched.
